title: How Artificial Intelligence Will Affect the Practice of Law
pub: University of Toronto Law Journal, vol. 68, supplement 1, pp. 106-124
author: Benjamin Alarie · Anthony Niblett · Albert H. Yoon

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Justice access: Direct AI use shifts risk downward
st.an: The source frames access to justice primarily as a consequence of lawyer-side productivity, lower task costs and redesigned service delivery. It does not assess the cluster’s central concern that direct-to-consumer AI transfers reliability and verification risks to unrepresented users, so it advances a materially different provider-focused account rather than the cluster’s risk-balancing proposition.
qs: For example, as legal work becomes less costly and more efficient, lawyers can charge less for discrete tasks while simultaneously accomplishing more work in the same amount of time.
In effect, artificial intelligence may increase access to civil and criminal justice in a way that benefits lawyers and clients alike.

st.t: Supervised AI: Verification may consume efficiency gains
st.an: The essay shifts the emphasis from verification-intensive, lifecycle-governed AI assistance to increasingly accurate predictive tools that improve productivity and may eventually become professionally required. It retains lawyers as decision-makers consulting AI, but does not substantively address the cluster’s central concerns about verification burdens, tool-specific reassessment or confidentiality controls.
qs: First, lawyers are able to do more in the same amount of time.

Looking further ahead, as predictive tools become more accurate, lawyers may not only come to rely on artificially intelligent tools, but may be legally required to consult these tools as part of their due diligence.

st.t: Human oversight: Accountability is not effective control
st.an: The source forecasts broad benefits from predictive AI, including efficiency, expertise and access gains, while acknowledging uncertain long-term effects. It does not substantively address whether human oversight provides effective control, requires independent verification, or risks weakening expertise, so its position on the cluster’s principal proposition cannot be determined.
qs: In the short term, the development of such predictive tools will improve transparency and empower lawyers to work more efficiently, deepen and broaden their areas of expertise, and provide greater access to justice and more value to clients.
In the longer term, it is unclear exactly how dramatic the impact of artificially intelligent tools will be.

st.t: Machine judging: Accuracy cannot establish legitimate authority
st.an: The source advocates AI assistance, partial task automation and litigation-outcome prediction, but does not address delegation of judicial authority or whether accuracy can confer adjudicative legitimacy. Its bounded scope is compatible with the cluster, yet it neither expressly accepts nor rejects the cluster’s principal proposition.
qs: We look to how natural language processing and machine learning can assist lawyers and perform some of the tasks currently undertaken by lawyers.

Such technological advances make it possible for parties to litigate more effectively, before, during, and after trial, by predicting legal outcomes with greater accuracy and consistency, and at lower cost.

st.t: Law-firm pyramid: Efficiency threatens revenue and training
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core account that client cost pressure and technology can restructure law-firm staffing and economics. It materially extends that account by identifying self-regulation, unauthorized-practice rules and possible protectionist rent seeking as additional factors that may slow or shape structural change, though it does not address the apprenticeship problem directly.
qs: partners at the top, and several rungs below to reflect the increasing variety of lawyer roles in the firm, ranging from non-equity partners, of-counsel, non-partner-track associates,15 contract lawyers,16 and outsourced lawyers.17  Client demand for lower legal expenses is only part of the story behind the evolution of private legal practice.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s task-reconfiguration and near-term augmentation thesis, emphasizing productivity in discrete predictive and production tasks rather than immediate wholesale lawyer replacement. It materially extends the proposition by arguing that substantial gains require redesigning legal-service delivery, although it gives little attention to verification, uneven user capability or apprenticeship risks and is more optimistic about accuracy and access-to-justice effects.
qs: We look to how natural language processing and machine learning can assist lawyers and perform some of the tasks currently undertaken by lawyers.

Taking the old system and simply inserting computers did little to improve productivity.52 Thus, the true benefits of artificially intelligent tools in the legal profession may be realized only once lawyers completely rethink the provision of legal services.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: The source accepts that technology and client cost pressure are transforming law-firm staffing and business models rather than simply eliminating lawyers. It materially extends the cluster by identifying technology as potentially profitable for equity partners and by analysing professional self-regulation and unauthorized-practice rules as institutional constraints on adoption.
qs: Technological advances provide the tools for law firms to facilitate this transition, and make it not only financially viable but also potentially lucrative for a firm’s equity partners.

st.t: Workflow unbundling: Buyers challenge time-based production
st.an: The source accepts that client cost pressure challenges hourly billing and reshapes firm staffing, then materially extends the synthesis by distinguishing the pre-AI impetus for restructuring from technology’s role in making alternative models financially viable. It is narrower than the cluster because it does not substantively address workflow-level allocation, junior training or verification risks.
qs: The economic downturn gave clients of law firms leverage to demand more cost-effective representation.12 Law firms began experimenting with alternative approaches, such as flat rates and contingency fees, in new contexts.
Technological advances provide the tools for law firms to facilitate this transition, and make it not only financially viable but also potentially lucrative for a firm’s equity partners.

st.t: Big Law economics: Durable value exceeds firm size
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s account of Big Law as undergoing client-driven restructuring rather than inevitable disappearance. It presents technology as an enabler of differentiated staffing and potentially higher equity-partner returns, while treating regulation as a contested influence on adoption rather than proof of incumbent replacement.
qs: In an effort to reduce operating expenses, law firms moved away from this traditional model.14 The emergence of non-equity partners (an intermediate step for associates in their initial promotion to partner) and increased numbers of of-counsel positions has transformed the “partnership tournament” into an “elastic tournament” with several gradations, with fewer paths to equity partnership.
Technological advances provide the tools for law firms to facilitate this transition, and make it not only financially viable but also potentially lucrative for a firm’s equity partners.

st.t: Billable hour: Faster matters need not reduce profits
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s institutional account of hourly billing: uncertain and evolving legal work helps explain persistence, while stronger client bargaining power has prompted alternative fees and organisational change. Its support is historical and structural; it does not directly assess whether AI-driven speed preserves profits.
qs: Moreover, completion of one legal task often gives rise to imperfectly anticipated subsequent legal tasks as the position and interests of clients evolve over time.

The economic downturn gave clients of law firms leverage to demand more cost-effective representation.12 Law firms began experimenting with alternative approaches, such as flat rates and contingency fees, in new contexts.

st.t: Firm tournament: Partnership extends rather than ends competition
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s account that client cost pressure has transformed the two-tier partnership tournament into a differentiated, elastic hierarchy with fewer routes to equity partnership. It also supports the cluster’s AI-era qualification that technology enables restructuring initiated and shaped by existing economic incentives, rather than determining organizational change by itself.
qs: In an effort to reduce operating expenses, law firms moved away from this traditional model.14 The emergence of non-equity partners (an intermediate step for associates in their initial promotion to partner) and increased numbers of of-counsel positions has transformed the “partnership tournament” into an “elastic tournament” with several gradations, with fewer paths to equity partnership.
Technological advances provide the tools for law firms to facilitate this transition, and make it not only financially viable but also potentially lucrative for a firm’s equity partners.

st.t: Legal automation: Classification success cannot prove reasoning
st.an: The source aligns with the cluster’s task-specific framing: it presents AI as assisting lawyers and automating some existing tasks, while identifying unstructured legal data as a central obstacle. Its optimism about litigation prediction is prospective rather than evidence that classification or retrieval establishes general legal reasoning competence.
qs: We look to how natural language processing and machine learning can assist lawyers and perform some of the tasks currently undertaken by lawyers.
A central challenge for using artificial intelligence in law is the unstructured nature of legal data.

st.t: Legal economics: AI makes adoption a model problem
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s central view that AI and related technology are business-model forces: client cost pressure prompts restructuring, while technology makes new staffing and economic arrangements viable and potentially profitable. Its discussion of regulatory resistance adds uncertainty about adoption speed but does not challenge the proposition.
qs: It provided the necessary impetus for law firms to transform their business model.
Technological advances provide the tools for law firms to facilitate this transition, and make it not only financially viable but also potentially lucrative for a firm’s equity partners.

st.t: Legal prediction: Classification cannot guarantee sound advice
st.an: The source treats predictive AI as bounded decision support that may improve discrete outcome assessments, not as a guarantee of sound legal advice or wholesale replacement for lawyers. It expressly limits suitability to questions with identifiable factors and sufficient data, while acknowledging increasing imprecision as legal complexity grows.
qs: We look to how natural language processing and machine learning can assist lawyers and perform some of the tasks currently undertaken by lawyers.
It is inappropriate in instances where the court’s determination of a legal question does not lend itself to an identifiable set of factors, or where insufficient data exist.

st.t: Legal workforce: Junior pipelines face the sharpest risk
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s central view that AI will augment lawyers and restructure legal-service delivery rather than clearly eliminate lawyers wholesale. It specifically anticipates pressure on billable-hour pricing and leveraged partner-associate staffing while acknowledging long-term uncertainty. However, it offers forecasts rather than empirical displacement evidence and does not specifically establish that junior training pipelines face the sharpest risk.
qs: In the short run, we can expect greater legal transparency, more efficient dispute resolution, improved access to justice, and new challenges to the traditional organization of private law firms delivering legal services on a billable hour basis through a leveraged partner-associate model.
With new technology, lawyers will be empowered to work more efficiently, deepen and broaden their areas of expertise, and provide more value to clients.

st.t: Partnership structure: AI tests governance beyond capital scarcity
st.an: The source supports the synthesis by treating technology as an enabler of organizational restructuring rather than proof that partnerships will disappear. It also links ownership and promotion to a more stratified staffing model and recognizes regulation as a potential constraint, while offering little evidence on capital scarcity, multidisciplinary governance or outside-investment outcomes.
qs: In an effort to reduce operating expenses, law firms moved away from this traditional model.14 The emergence of non-equity partners (an intermediate step for associates in their initial promotion to partner) and increased numbers of of-counsel positions has transformed the “partnership tournament” into an “elastic tournament” with several gradations, with fewer paths to equity partnership.
Technological advances provide the tools for law firms to facilitate this transition, and make it not only financially viable but also potentially lucrative for a firm’s equity partners.

st.t: Value capture: Integrated delivery reshapes market boundaries
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s proposition that technology-driven value capture depends on restructuring legal delivery rather than merely accelerating tasks. It links client cost pressure, diversified staffing and technological capability to business-model change and potential gains for equity partners, while treating regulatory resistance as a conditional constraint rather than rejecting transformation.
qs: partners at the top, and several rungs below to reflect the increasing variety of lawyer roles in the firm, ranging from non-equity partners, of-counsel, non-partner-track associates,15 contract lawyers,16 and outsourced lawyers.17  Client demand for lower legal expenses is only part of the story behind the evolution of private legal practice.
Technological advances provide the tools for law firms to facilitate this transition, and make it not only financially viable but also potentially lucrative for a firm’s equity partners.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source aligns with the cluster’s core view that AI delivers gains in bounded legal tasks and that substantial value requires redesigning legal-service delivery rather than merely accelerating existing workflows. It is more optimistic about predictive systems challenging human judgment and improving access, but conditions these benefits on accuracy and treats longer-term substitution as uncertain; it provides little support for the cluster’s stronger emphasis on verification and interaction design.
qs: If legal classifiers are able to provide accurate predictions for discrete questions of law, lawyers can take advantage of them in a variety of ways.

Taking the old system and simply inserting computers did little to improve productivity.52 Thus, the true benefits of artificially intelligent tools in the legal profession may be realized only once lawyers completely rethink the provision of legal services.

kp.k: Predictive AI promises augmentation, not immediate lawyer replacement
kp.d: The authors primarily examine machine learning for assessing discrete legal issues, predicting greater consistency, lower costs and less susceptibility to lawyers’ experiential and client-driven biases. Their short-term account treats these tools as legal information rather than comprehensive legal advice; the longer-term impact remains uncertain.
qs: Machine learning has the potential to provide more objective predictions of how courts will decide discrete legal issues.
They do not purport to offer legal advice in the same way that lawyers do.
Accordingly, these tools do not supplant what lawyers fundamentally do on behalf of their clients.

kp.k: Post-recession client pressure challenged hourly billing and traditional leverage
kp.d: The authors describe post-2008 pressure for cheaper, more predictable representation as an existing driver of change, not an effect established as caused by AI. Firms experimented with flat rates and contingency fees and diversified career tiers, reducing paths to equity partnership. Technology is presented as enabling this transition and potentially increasing equity-partner profitability.
qs: Law firms have traditionally tended to provide legal services on a billable hour basis and, at large law firms, to leverage large numbers of associates for each law firm partner.

The emergence of non-equity partners (an intermediate step for associates in their initial promotion to partner) and increased numbers of of-counsel positions has transformed the “partnership tournament” into an “elastic tournament” with several gradations, with fewer paths to equity partnership.
Technological advances provide the tools for law firms to facilitate this transition, and make it not only financially viable but also potentially lucrative for a firm’s equity partners.

kp.k: Computational research moves beyond faster access toward synthesis
kp.d: The essay distinguishes analog, digital and computational legal information. Digital research accelerated searching without guaranteeing quality and retained cost and search-precision barriers. The authors envision computational tools adding synthesis and outcome prediction rather than merely making existing documents easier to retrieve.
qs: Access was necessary, but by no means sufficient, for quality legal representation.
A keyword search poses the risk of being under- and over-inclusive in defining the scope of relevant materials.
This stage involves the use of predictive tools to sort through noise and more easily locate and synthesize relevant information.

kp.k: Document automation already reduces routine legal labour
kp.d: The authors report existing applications in discovery, contract review and analysis, litigation-data structuring and bankruptcy research. Citing Remus and Levy, they state that lawyers spend less than 5 percent of their time on basic document review. Their discovery discussion cites a journalistic comparison of a 1978 case involving 6 million documents costing $2.2 million with a 2011 case involving 1.5 million documents costing less than $100,000; these are different cases, not a controlled productivity comparison.
qs: Because most legal documents now originate in electronic format, the discovery process can now be conducted with a fraction of the time, expense, and need for lawyers, with even greater accuracy.
lawyers now spend less than 5 percent of their time on basic document review.
The software also facilitates the interpretation of existing contracts, in response to or in anticipation of litigation.

kp.k: Legal prediction requires costly upfront data structuring
kp.d: The authors identify heterogeneous, contextual judicial writing as an obstacle to extraction and prediction, especially for complex questions. Their proposed approach defines a discrete question, identifies relevant documents and extracts features with lawyers, machine-learning experts and developers. They argue that these front-loaded costs enable comparatively inexpensive application and scalable access afterward.
qs: Accordingly, algorithms relying on natural language process may yield imprecise results, and predictably more so as the complexity of the legal question increases.
This process may be labour intensive, requiring the inputs of lawyers, machine learning experts, and developers to complete each stage.
This process, while costly, is front-loaded.
The cost of applying machine learning to this data – now structured – is modest by comparison.

kp.k: Blue J illustrates bounded, fact-intensive legal classification
kp.d: The authors describe their own company’s Canadian tax-law classifiers, disclosing that all three are co-founders. The workflow codes published decisions into structured factors and predicts binary legal outcomes, including employee versus independent-contractor status. Outputs include a predicted outcome, percentage likelihood, explanatory memo, leading decisions and factually similar precedents. This is a product-method description, not a reported accuracy evaluation.
qs: Blue J Legal uses machine learning to build tax law classifiers, based on published Supreme Court of Canada, Federal Court of Appeal, and Tax Court of Canada decisions, in which the court makes a binary determination for a specific legal question.
The next step is to code every published decision in accordance with the aforementioned factors.
In the interests of full disclosure, we reiterate that the three co-authors are also co-founders of Blue J Legal.

kp.k: Insufficient data and unclear factors limit suitable applications
kp.d: The authors explicitly reject universal application of predictive tools. Their account requires legal questions with identifiable decision factors and sufficient data. Whether future developments can overcome these limitations is left open.
qs: The temptation of artificial intelligence is to view it as a proverbial hammer where all the legal questions are nails.
The law does not fit this paradigm.
It is inappropriate in instances where the court’s determination of a legal question does not lend itself to an identifiable set of factors, or where insufficient data exist.

kp.k: Lawyers retain problem framing, factual judgment and holistic advice
kp.d: The authors distinguish answering isolated legal questions from identifying the right questions and advising on clients’ wider interests. They argue that lawyers must assess the accuracy of asserted facts and the suitability of the technology. Their medical analogy suggests that informed self-help can improve on no assistance but does not replace a professional using AI.
qs: She identifies the appropriate question (or likely, multiple questions) to answer.
Moreover, her task is to advise a course of action that goes beyond the specific and immediate legal question, to consider the client’s overall circumstances and interests.

A lawyer who uses artificial intelligence will still need to exercise her reasoned judgment to evaluate the accuracy of the purported facts, as well as the appropriateness of the technology in resolving the legal dispute.

kp.k: Shared predictions could improve settlement and litigation strategy
kp.d: Conditional on accurate predictions, the authors expect plaintiffs and defendants to gain timely assessments generated through common methods. They predict greater legal transparency throughout settlement, trial preparation and appeals, with disagreements narrowed toward pivotal facts that evidence can resolve.
qs: If legal classifiers are able to provide accurate predictions for discrete questions of law, lawyers can take advantage of them in a variety of ways.
More importantly, each side can benefit from the same methods of generating these assessments.
These classifiers can help parties focus on pivotal fact-based areas of disagreement, which can be more easily overcome with evidence.

kp.k: Government could use classifiers to allocate litigation resources
kp.d: The authors propose government use for consistent advice, deciding whether to challenge or settle administrative claims, and identifying strengths, weaknesses and consequential factual issues in litigation. These are prospective applications intended to improve decisions under limited budgets.
qs: Government can also use legal classifiers to help evaluate claims and manage litigation risk.
For administrative claims, the government can use the classifier to determine whether they should challenge the claim or simply settle.
In so doing, the government can deploy limited litigation resources more efficiently.

kp.k: AI could weaken scale advantages and broaden lawyer expertise
kp.d: The authors predict three effects: more work or clients per unit of time, reduced dependence on large firms’ labour resources, and broader rather than progressively narrower specialization. These are projected competitive and occupational consequences, not measured staffing or employment outcomes.
qs: Their increased efficiency can enable them to perform additional work on behalf of existing clients, or perhaps help more clients.
Smaller firms can perform as capably as larger firms, since artificial intelligence increasingly obviates the need for massive labour power emblematic of large law firms.
Third, lawyers may be able to broaden rather than narrow their areas of specialization.

kp.k: Regulation could resist adoption or eventually require predictive tools
kp.d: The essay reports disagreement over whether professional self-regulation can obstruct machine intelligence: some scholars anticipate resistance, while McGinnis and Pearce argue unauthorized-practice laws will not preserve lawyers’ monopoly. Separately, the authors speculate that increasingly accurate tools could become part of legally required diligence, exposing lawyers to negligence claims for failing to consult or appropriately heed them. They do not describe such a duty as existing law.
qs: They argue that the unauthorized practice laws are rarely applied successfully to machine intelligence products.

Looking further ahead, as predictive tools become more accurate, lawyers may not only come to rely on artificially intelligent tools, but may be legally required to consult these tools as part of their due diligence.
A lawyer, by failing to access the most accurate legal information or failing to use predictive tools to better assess how a case will develop, may expose herself professional liability in tort.

kp.k: Major productivity gains may require organizational redesign
kp.d: Using historical accounts of electrification and workplace computing as analogies, the authors argue that substituting technology into unchanged processes may yield limited benefits. They suggest that rethinking legal-service delivery could let lawyers lower charges for discrete tasks while performing more work, potentially improving access to civil and criminal justice. This is a proposed mechanism rather than an observed legal-sector result.
qs: The explosion in productivity came later when firms restructured their systems, architecture, logistics, and personnel to take advantage of the new technology.
Thus, the true benefits of artificially intelligent tools in the legal profession may be realized only once lawyers completely rethink the provision of legal services.
In effect, artificial intelligence may increase access to civil and criminal justice in a way that benefits lawyers and clients alike.

kp.k: Bail research illustrates potential algorithmic decision improvements
kp.d: The authors cite Kleinberg and colleagues’ February 2017 NBER working paper on New York bail hearings as evidence of potential benefits beyond legal-service production. They report alternative projected outcomes—25% less crime without increasing the jail population, or a 42% smaller jail population without increasing crime—not realized effects of an implemented reform.
qs: A recent study of bail hearings in New York found that machine learning algorithms may reduce crime by 25% without increasing the jail population or reduce the jail population by 42% without increasing the crime rate.

kp.k: Personalized law could transform lawyers into policy advisers
kp.d: Drawing on other scholarship, the authors explore a longer-term possibility in which algorithms reshape lawmaking itself, tailoring law to individual circumstances and blurring rules and standards. They speculate that direct communication of personalized laws could shift lawyers away from advising individual clients toward policy advice, while expressly acknowledging uncertainty about long-term effects.
qs: Other work has explored how other lawmakers can use artificial intelligence to make laws that are better tailored to individual circumstances, blurring the line between rules and standards and providing for increased personalization of law.

In such a world where specific laws are highly personalized and communicated to individuals directly, the role of a lawyer may transform to one of a policy advisor, rather than an advisor of individual clients.
In the longer term, it is unclear exactly how dramatic the impact of artificially intelligent tools will be.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Alarie, Niblett and Yoon predict that computational legal tools will improve prediction, productivity and dispute resolution, challenge traditional firm economics, and potentially transform legal services and lawmaking.
pts.d: The authors describe e-discovery as already reducing document-review time, expense and demand for lawyers, and describe software supporting contract drafting, interpretation and legal research. Their principal prediction is that machine learning can provide more objective, consistent, replicable and less costly assessments of discrete legal questions. Shared predictive methods could help litigants identify pivotal factual disagreements and resolve disputes more efficiently, while governments could use classifiers to assess claims, decide whether to settle and allocate litigation resources. They expect lawyers to handle more work, broaden expertise and operate effectively in smaller firms, challenging the billable-hour and leveraged partner-associate model. In the short term, they frame these tools as augmenting rather than replacing lawyers: lawyers still identify the appropriate questions, assess facts and advise on clients’ broader interests. They suggest that sufficiently accurate predictive tools could eventually become part of legally required professional due diligence. Longer-term possibilities include redesigning legal-service delivery, lowering task prices and expanding access to justice, algorithmically supported regulation and adjudication, and personalized laws that could shift lawyers toward policy advice.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The essay supports its predictions with existing applications, the authors’ Blue J Legal experience, cited research and reporting, and historical analogies; it does not report a new quantitative evaluation of its overall predictions.
pts.d: For discovery, the authors cite reporting comparing a 1978 review of six million documents costing $2.2 million with a 2011 review of 1.5 million documents costing less than $100,000. They cite Remus and Levy for the statement that lawyers spend less than 5 percent of their time on basic document review. Product examples include Kira Systems for contracts and Brainspace for structuring litigation-related data. The principal predictive-law example is Blue J Legal, which all three authors disclose they co-founded. They describe identifying discrete Canadian tax-law questions, coding published decisions into structured factors, and producing classifiers that return outcomes, probabilities, explanatory memoranda and relevant precedents. This is an account of system development and functionality, not a numerical accuracy benchmark in this essay. For judicial applications, they cite the February 2017 Kleinberg and colleagues working paper’s estimates that algorithms could reduce crime by 25 percent without increasing the jail population, or reduce the jail population by 42 percent without increasing crime. These are attributed research estimates, not reported effects of a completed deployment. Their argument that larger productivity gains require organizational redesign draws on historical research about electrification and workplace computers. Claims about professional liability, broader expertise, smaller-firm competitiveness and future lawyer roles are prospective arguments rather than measured outcomes.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The authors distinguish applications already present in the 2017–2018 context from short-term augmentation and explicitly uncertain longer-term transformation.
pts.d: The article, published in 2018 with a manuscript citation dated November 2017, treats e-discovery, contract tools and initial tax classifiers as existing developments. Its short-term predictions concern productivity, legal transparency, litigation management and access, without specifying a calendar deadline. Benefits from legal classifiers are conditional on accurate predictions for discrete questions. The authors emphasize the difficulty of extracting information from unstructured judicial opinions, increasing imprecision with legal complexity, and the substantial initial work needed to structure data. They exclude questions lacking identifiable decision factors or sufficient data from the appropriate present scope of these tools. Lawyers must still assess purported facts and whether a tool is suitable for a dispute. Professional-liability predictions depend on predictive tools becoming more accurate and standards of due diligence evolving. They also identify professional self-regulation and possible strengthening of unauthorized-practice restrictions as adoption barriers, while separately reporting McGinnis and Pearce’s more optimistic view of overcoming such barriers. Longer-term productivity gains may require wholesale service redesign rather than simply substituting software into existing processes. Personalized law and a shift toward policy advice are possibilities, not dated or unconditional forecasts.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The projected effects extend to private practitioners and firms, clients and litigants, government decision-makers, judges and people needing legal help.
pts.d: The discussion of firm organization focuses on private legal services in Canada and the United States. Junior associates and document reviewers face reduced demand for routine review work; the authors do not quantify aggregate lawyer job losses. Partners and large firms face pressure on staffing leverage and hourly billing, although technology-enabled changes could also benefit equity partners financially. Small firms could compete more effectively without large associate workforces, and individual lawyers could serve additional clients and maintain broader expertise. Plaintiffs and defendants could obtain earlier, more consistent assessments of their positions. Government agents, auditors and lawyers could make more consistent decisions and allocate limited litigation budgets more efficiently. Public-interest and government organizations are described as having strong incentives to adopt cost-saving tools under budget constraints. People unable to obtain legal help could benefit if efficiency translates into lower prices and greater service capacity; this access claim is distinct from enterprise cost savings. Judges and criminal defendants are implicated by predictive bail tools, while regulators and the public could be affected by more transparent or personalized law. The authors’ central near-term account retains lawyers as advisers rather than positioning litigants’ direct use of classifiers as an equivalent replacement.
